Oral Judgment :

This Criminal Appeal is preferred by the Appellant-State against the judgment and order dated 27.08.2002 delivered by learned Judicial Magistrate First Class, Kelapur, in Regular Criminal Case No.43/1993, whereby the learned trial Judge has acquitted the accused under Sections 16 (1) (a) (ii)
read with Section 7 (1) read with Section 2 (ia)
(a) and Section 7 (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 appeal 197.03 ("Act" for short) read with Section 2(ix) (d) Rule 23 of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 ("Rules" for short).

sentences.text:
1 2 . The prosecution case, in nutshell, can be summarised as under:
One Shri J.K. Kamble, who was the Food Inspector, visited to shop of the accused,
who is the Proprietor of M/s. Jalaram Traders, Matanagar, Ralegaon,
District-Yavatmal, was engaged in stocking for sale and selling of food articles from that shop.

It is the case of the prosecution that the accused was not holding a license,
as required for conducting the said business of selling food articles.

On 13.11.1992 at about 11.30 a.m. the Food Inspector - Shri J.K.Kamble visited to M/s Jalaram Traders and disclosed his identity to the accused; so also his intention of drawing samples of food articles for the purpose of analysis.
He purchased 600 grams of "Saunf" from the accused in presence of witnesses from an open bag containing 50 Kgs., Saunf kept for sale.
The price of the said sample was paid to the Shopkeeper.
Thereafter, Shri Kamble gave a notice in Form-VI to the accused in presence of witnesses.
He also gave a notice under Section 14-A of the Act to the accused and obtained their reply.
Mr.Kamble then issued sample of Saunf so sold to him, as per the procedure laid down in the Act and the Rules, under a panchanama.

He has sent one sealed part of the sample along with original Memorandum appeal 197.03 in Form-VII in a sealed packet to the Public Analyst, State Health Laboratory, Pune, for analysis on 16.11.1992 by Registered Post A.D., under intimation to the Local Health Authority and the Assistant Commissioner, Food and Drugs Administration, M.S.Yavatmal.
He also sent a copy of the Memorandum in Form VII along with specimen impression of seal used to seal the sample in a sealed packet to the Public Analyst, Public Health Laboratory, Pune.
Other parts of two samples along with two copies of Memorandum in Form-VII in a sealed packet were sent to the Local Health Authority, Yavatmal, on the same day.

On 08.01.1993, Shri Kamble received a report of the Public Analyst, which indicated that the sample containing extraneous non permitted green colouring matter and did not confirm to the standards of Saunf, as per Rules, 1955.

Shri Kamble then submitted all the papers to the Assistant Commissioner, Food and Drugs Administration, M.S.Yavatmal, which was forwarded to the Joint Commissioner, M.S. Nagpur,
under Section 20 of the Act.
The complainant then filed complaint against the accused under the provisions of the Act.

3. The learned trial Judge, after recording evidence and hearing of both sides, acquitted the accused,
as mentioned in paragraph 1 above.
4.
I have heard learned Additional Public Prosecutor appearing appeal 197.03 for the appellant-State and the learned Advocate appearing for the respondent.
With their able assistance, I have gone through the entire record and proceedings of the case.

5. The learned Additional Public Prosecutor vehemently argued that the learned trial Judge has not assessed and appreciated the evidence led by the prosecution in its right perspective and has erroneously acquitted the accused.

sentences.text: 2 6. As against this, the learned Advocate for the respondent supported the impugned judgment and order delivered by the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class and contended that the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class has rightly acquitted the accused.

7. On a perusal of the impugned judgment and order passed by the trial Court, it is noticed that the learned Judicial Magistrate First Class has fairly discussed the reasons for acquittal of the accused.
The evidence on record shows that the Food Inspector had divided the said sample into three parts without actual measurement, however, it is not divided actually by weighing the samples.
As per the provisions under Section 11 (b) of the Act, the Food Inspector has to divide the sample into three parts, however, three samples were not divided equally by weighing it.
Thus, there is failure on the part of the Food Inspector Shri appeal 197.03 Jagdish Kamble to comply with the provisions under Section 11 (b) of the Act.
8. It is further noticed that Rule 22 of the Rules, which provides that minimum quantity of samples is to be sent to Public Analyst, is not complied with.
So, Saunf is not specified in the table given in Rule 22 of the Rules.
However, in case of unspecified commodities, the minimum commodity of sample to be sent to the Public Analyst is 500 grams.
For species, the minimum quantity is 150 grams.
Thus, even if we include Saunf in the category of spices, then at least 150 grams of Saunf should have been sent for analysis.

However, in the instant case, the sample was not divided by weighting it and, therefore, it cannot be said that minimum quantity of Saunf was sent to the Public Analyst, as per the requirements of Rule 22 of the Rules.
Thus, the said mandatory requirement has not been followed by the Food Inspector.
9. It is also noticed that the sealing of samples was not done properly.

The evidence of the Food Inspector shows that he did not send the samples by weighing it and thus, he has completely ignored the provisions of the Rules and not followed Rule 22 of the Rules by sending minimum quantity of sample to the Public Analyst for analysis.
Therefore, it is doubtful that whether the articles were properly sealed or not.

It is further noticed that the provisions under Section 13 (2A) of appeal 197.03 the Act, are not complied with, as the remaining part of sample was not deposited in the Court within a stipulated period.
The Food Inspector was supposed to forward the part of the sample to the Court within a period of five days from the date of receipt of requisition.
The said provision is also not complied with by the Food Inspector.
10. The overall assessment of the evidence shows that since the mandatory provisions under the Act and the Rules were not complied with, the accused has been rightly acquitted by the trial Court.

11. In the case of Mahendra Pratap Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh, reported in (2009) 11 SCC 334,
the Hon'ble Apex Court has given a rule of prudence that if on appraisal of evidence and on considering relevant attending circumstances, it is found that two views are possible, one for acquitting accused and other for convicting accused, in such a situation, rule of prudence should guide High Court not to disturb the order of acquittal made by the trial court, unless conclusions of trial court drawn on evidence on record are found to be unreasonable and perverse or unsustainable, High Court should not interfere with the order of acquittal.
